The rapid expansion of the digital world has significantly altered the way people interact with the government, shifting it towards a more service-oriented, digital platform. This shift has created an urgent need for an open-domain Question Answering system that can provide clear, concise responses to users' inquiries. In this research, we introduce an innovative, transformer-based framework designed to address this requirement. This model can effectively process a broad spectrum of questions, leveraging a large corpus of documents to yield accurate and precise answers. Through rigorous testing on a public dataset, we demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, showcasing its robustness in handling diverse question types. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of this technology to revolutionize public service by integrating it with an Ethiopian government hotline.

Recent observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation have led researchers to reconsider the "missing baryons" problem. A possible solution to this issue is the presence of warm dark matter. A study of the galaxy cluster, EAGLE, and its properties has been conducted to explore the effects of different mass functions on the formation of cosmic structures. A comparison of the results with observations of the XMM-Newton survey reveals that a warm dark matter model with a mass of 6.7 kiloparsecs per second can better explain the data. Furthermore, the results show that a warm dark matter model can also account for the observed properties of the galaxy cluster, M~1871, without requiring the presence of a massive, dark matter subhalo.

We present an algorithm that identifies all leftmost separators of a given graph G with a specified size, k or less. A leftmost separator of a graph is a vertex or set of vertices that divides the graph's connected components into two distinct groups, while minimizing the distance between these groups. Our algorithm, which is based on a concept by Khit'ovich and Musatov, runs in a polynomial time of O(n + m) when applied to an undirected graph, and in a polynomial time of O(m) when applied to a directed graph. Additionally, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be used to identify all minimal separators of a graph with a specified size, with our method taking O(n + m) time.

We have analyzed the light curves of 175 galaxies hosting 268 transient events. These transients were identified within 12.6 years of photometric data in the SDSS DR8 database. Our sample includes 175 galaxies that were post-starburst at the time of observation, 32 galaxies classified as quiescent, and 5 galaxies with no observed star formation. We have found that the frequency of transients in post-starburst galaxies is 2.5 times higher than in quiescent galaxies. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the rate of transients in post-starburst galaxies is primarily due to the higher rate of type IIn events in these galaxies. We have also observed that the brightness of transients in post-starburst galaxies is 0.4 magnitudes higher than in quiescent galaxies. Our findings indicate that the presence of post-starburst galaxies is associated with an increased rate of transients, particularly type IIn events.

In reconfigurable wireless networks, the ability to dynamically adjust transmission settings plays a crucial role in optimizing resource allocation. A key challenge is determining the most suitable transmission mode for a given application based on factors like power consumption, network capacity, and end-to-end quality of service. This paper presents a novel scheduling framework, which leverages actor-critic reinforcement learning to strike a balance between power efficiency and network capacity while ensuring quality of service constraints are met. The proposed framework comprises two deep learning agents: one focused on minimizing power consumption and the other on network capacity. Their respective reward functions are designed to prevent the overemphasis on one objective at the expense of the other, thus promoting a more balanced approach. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms traditional methods in terms of network capacity and power efficiency.

The translation post-editing process can be significantly improved with the assistance of automatic word-level quality estimation, which helps post-editors identify reliable machine translation output and prioritize low-quality areas for further correction. However, existing word-level quality estimation models often struggle to accurately predict high-quality words produced by the MT system, leading to unnecessary post-editing work. In this research, we introduce a new word-level quality estimation model that leverages the strengths of recent QE models in combination with a cutting-edge cross-lingual post-editing model. By using the cross-lingual model to generate quality labels for each word and training on these labels, our new model is able to accurately predict high-quality words produced by the MT system and provide more effective post-editing guidance. Experimental results on WMT19 QE shared task demonstrate that our new model outperforms existing word-level quality estimation models in most cases, with a notable improvement of 1.1 BLEU points in post-editing tasks.

The shadow size of a black hole is influenced by its spin and the surrounding cosmological context, particularly the value of the cosmological constant. By analyzing how the shadow changes in response to the cosmological constant, researchers have found that they can determine the value of the constant with significant accuracy by measuring the change in central disk brightness and ring obscurations. Using the Planck data, the team calculated the shadow size of black holes in the universe and found that the size is consistent with different values of the cosmological constant, with the size depending on the constant in a specific way. The team then used the shadow size to estimate the value of the constant and found that it is consistent with the value obtained from Planck data, with the size indicating a specific value of the constant that is consistent with the value obtained from Planck data, with further study indicating that the shadow size can be used to test and refine the value of the constant in the context of the Kerr-de Sitter spacetime.

A novel method has been developed to solve the relativistic Navier-Stokes equations numerically, particularly for complex, expanding plasma systems. This approach is based on a newly formulated set of equations that streamlines the resolution of plasma interactions in multiple directions, significantly reducing the computational burden associated with N-dimensional plasma systems. This formulation has been successfully applied to a simplified 2D plasma system and yielded a substantial reduction in computational time compared to traditional methods, when both systems had the same number of grid points. This accelerated solution enables more efficient analysis of plasma dynamics and can facilitate the study of plasma interactions in various contexts.

The LHCb experiment analyzed proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies to study the $D^{(*)+}_{sJ}$ mesons' decays to $D^{*+} K^0_{\rm S}$ and $D^{*0} K^+$ final states. The data consisted of 0.63 and 7.0 fb^-1, which were used to determine the $D^{*+}_{s1}$ and $D^{*+}_{sJ}$ (with J=2) masses and their ratios to $D^+_{s}$, with the results being 2974.1±0.9±0.4 MeV and 4001.2±0.9±0.4 MeV, and 0.045±0.008±0.004 and 0.035±0.008±0.004 respectively.

This paper delves into various types of fractal polynomials within the context of the Sierpi\'nski gasket. We demonstrate the continuous fractal embedding of these polynomials within function spaces. Our results also reveal the fractal dimension of polynomial spaces. Furthermore, we investigate the fractal dimension of the graph of polynomial functions.

Visual question generation involves creating questions that relate to visual content, which is a complex task requiring a deep understanding of images and the underlying grammar of language. While significant progress has been made, existing approaches often struggle with producing coherent and relevant questions. This paper proposes a novel visual question generation framework that leverages a pre-trained image encoder and a language model to better understand image content and language structure, thereby generating more accurate and semantic questions. By incorporating a visual attention mechanism, our method can focus on the most important image regions when answering visual questions. Additionally, our approach includes a question generation module that learns to predict the most likely question type based on the image and the most important image regions. Experimental results on the VizWiz and COCO-VQG datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming state-of-the-art models in terms of question relevance and the ability to accurately identify image regions.

The transformation of dark matter haloes from cusp-like to core-like structures is a long-standing issue in the field of astrophysics and astrophysical cosmology. The process of cusp-core transformation is crucial for understanding the evolution of galaxies and the origin of various astrophysical phenomena, including the suppression of star-formation and the occurrence of gravitational waves. The concept of self-interacting dark matter has been proposed as a potential solution to explain cusp-core transformation. The process of cusp-core transformation is closely related to the process of supernova-driven core collapse, which involves the transformation of dark matter haloes. The process of supernova-driven core collapse is a fundamental mechanism for cusp-core transformation. The purpose of this review is to discuss the current understanding of cusp-core transformation and the role of supernova-driven core collapse in this process.

This research paper presents novel methods for eliminating quantifiers at a complex, second-order logical level, by adapting techniques used in propositional satisfiability problems. Our approach incorporates two new methods: a second-order variant of the resolution rule and a novel application of the hyper-resolution rule. These techniques have been successfully implemented within the TPS theorem-prover and have been tested on several real-world examples. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the proposed method can outperform existing second-order elimination methods in several cases.

In a multi-type system, the average population distribution over different types can be modeled using a replicator equation, especially when the system's dynamics are represented by a similar-order preserving mapping. We identify necessary and sufficient conditions for the stability of these equations in the multi-dimensional space. Additionally, the stability analysis is extended to include the study of nearly stable systems. Furthermore, the stability results are applied to a specific example: the maximum population size across different types. We also explore the emergence of historical paths in replicator equations, especially when the system's dynamics are represented by a C-pseudo convex mapping.

Random Forests, a prominent machine learning method, remain largely unconnected to more established statistical practices within the field. To bridge this gap, we develop a theoretical framework that allows us to derive the precise distribution of Random Forest-based estimators under specific conditions, enabling the creation of large-sample normal confidence intervals and standard errors for a range of parameters. The proposed method is applied to a regression context involving response functions that can be nonlinear and handle diverse types of data, including both discrete and continuous variables. The theoretical framework is further demonstrated through the analysis of a diverse set of examples, showcasing the method's utility and efficiency in practical applications.

A surge in electric vehicles can lead to uneven current distribution in the power grid, potentially resulting in overheating and grid damage. To mitigate this, vehicle charging can be managed through the smart charging technique, but this requires the electric vehicles to constantly share their charging needs with the grid operator and receive instructions in return. To minimize communication between the grid operator and the electric vehicles, a new method called Communication-Censored-ADMM is proposed. This method uses a censored communication approach, where the electric vehicles only send updates to the grid operator when there is a significant change in their power requirements, thus reducing communication overhead. The proposed scheme is shown to converge to the optimal solution, even with the electric vehicles' updates delayed, and is demonstrated to offer significant improvements in communication efficiency through numerical simulations.

Using first-principles calculations based on density functional theory, researchers have employed the hybrid functional approach to investigate the structural, elastic, and electronic characteristics of the perovskite compound SmFeO3. By examining the crystal structure, band structure, and density of states, the study found that SmFeO3 has a distorted orthorhombic phase with a certain degree of magnetism, and that this phase is metallic. Furthermore, the study found that SmFeO3 has a certain degree of magnetism, and that its elastic properties are within a certain range. By comparing the calculated properties to existing data, the study found that SmFeO3 has a certain degree of magnetism, and that its elastic properties are in agreement with experimental results.

The "ways of life" concept, initially developed by anthropologists, suggests that organisms' lifestyles are shaped by their environments and are driven by their need for survival. This concept can be applied to the study of bacteria, where various factors such as growth rate, reproduction, and movement influence their existence. By examining these factors, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of bacteria and uncover underlying patterns in their lifestyles. This study presents a new, interactive visualization tool that allows users to map the lifestyles of bacteria and identify relationships between different factors that impact their existence.

A new approach has been developed for modelling smart building ventilation systems, which focuses on identifying the optimal control strategy for an aerosolizing subcategory. The approach involves using measured data to create a model of the system, consisting of two stages: first, a simplified model is built using principal component analysis and NARX models, and then, a detailed model is developed using genetic programming. The resulting model can be used in a nonlinear MPC controller to determine the optimal control inputs for the system. The approach was successfully tested on a simulated aerosolizing ventilation system, with the results showing that the MVA-based model accurately captured the system's dynamics and the NMPC controller effectively optimized the control inputs.

The underlying physics behind superluminous supernovae remains a mystery, with researchers exploring two main formation mechanisms. One involves massive star collapse, while the other involves interactions between a compact object and its surrounding material. A third scenario, involving the merger of two stars, is also possible. A recent study of the extremely luminous Type I supernova 2017gci has provided new insights into its origin. Data suggests that the explosion occurred in a binary system, with a companion star identified as a low-mass helium star. Analysis of the star's mass and the time it took for the explosion suggests that the companion star was likely a low-mass, helium-rich star. A simulation of the star's evolution indicates that the star likely lost its hydrogen-rich envelope, with a small chance of the star merging with a companion star before exploding. A different simulation suggests that the star may have transferred mass to a companion star, with a low mass ratio, resulting in a merger.

A two-dimensional single-domain magnet is described by a quantum version of the classical Stoner-Wohlfarth model, in which spin and magnetization are treated as fundamental entities. The model's Hamiltonian is constructed using a spin operator based on the Dirac monopole in a 2D space with topological charge defined by the scalar curvature. The model's predictions for magnetization distribution and related physical quantities around an isolated magnetic vortex/singularity align with recent experiments measuring the second-harmonic generation signal.

A novel, neural-based approach to syntactic dependency parsing is introduced, which incorporates a unique graph structure that captures both syntactic and semantic attributes. This innovative framework enables the disentanglement of syntactic and semantic tasks, allowing for more accurate and comprehensive parsing of complex word sequences. By leveraging a visual representation of the dependency tree, the model can efficiently process multi-token words and achieve optimal performance. Experimental evaluations on English and German datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding superior results compared to existing methods.

Recent breakthroughs in feature attribution have enabled a deeper understanding of complex deep learning models by identifying the most influential input variables. Despite this progress, there's a lack of research evaluating the effectiveness of these methods, particularly when applied to computer vision tasks. In this work, we bridge this gap by thoroughly assessing the validity of five prominent feature attribution methods in the image domain, employing a multi-faceted approach that considers both local and global attributions. Our results indicate that these methods can produce varying levels of agreement among each other, with some methods performing better than others.

We investigate the stability of a thin-shell wormhole in a static, non-symmetric spacetime that has two distinct shadows. The wormhole's solution was previously derived using a different method. In this study, we examine the linear stability of this wormhole solution. We find that a wormhole with a double image capability can be stable when a specific condition is met, namely that the Schwarzschild metric lies outside the wormhole metric. This condition is necessary for the wormhole to have two separate shadows. If this condition is not met, the wormhole model is unphysical.

This study delves into the relationship between the entropy of a sequence generated by an i.i.d. random walk and the permutation's ranking within the longest-increasing-subsequence hierarchy. We establish that a particular entropy function, tied to Euler's partition function and its derivatives, serves as a valid entropy function for the random walk in question. Additionally, we demonstrate that the permutation's entropy relative to the walk's entropy is directly proportional to the length of the longest-increasing-subsequence length (Aldous' permutation statistic), up to a constant factor, for all relevant parameters. This finding is extended to the more general case of Markov chains with stationary, ergodic transitions.

The trimer map, a planar graph with three-degree vertices, has been extensively studied in terms of domino tilings, where each face represents an open or closed region, creating a pattern of alternating open and closed areas.  In a typical domino tiling, this area alternates between open and closed regions, creating a consistent pattern of alternating open and closed areas.  In this context, the problem of determining the number of trimer maps with a specific structure, known as a "gromov polyhedral graph", has been of particular interest. Domain adaptation, a long-standing challenge, has seen significant advancements with the emergence of self-training methods, which have shown impressive performance in various settings. Nonetheless, existing self-training approaches face two primary issues: 1) they heavily rely on the quality of the source domain data, and 2) they lack the ability to effectively utilize target domain data. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel self-training framework that leverages the strengths of prototype-based and reciprocal approaches. This framework utilizes data points from both domains to learn class-aware prototypes and reciprocal points. The reciprocal points are then used to generate pseudo-labellers, and this process is iteratively repeated to improve the accuracy of the learned models. Our proposed framework, called ProtoRec, has been extensively tested on multiple benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This research introduces a novel pose estimation and 3D reconstruction approach for vehicles in stereo images using a customized shape model. The method is tailored for vehicle pose estimation in autonomous driving scenarios, where the incorporation of a precise vehicle shape model enhances accuracy. To address the limitations of existing methods in utilizing shape priors, we developed a subcategory-agnostic shape model that enables efficient learning and adaptation. The approach starts by creating a comprehensive database of various vehicle types with corresponding shape models, followed by training a neural network to predict the parameters of the shape model based on vehicle poses. The method then utilizes a stereo image to estimate the vehicle's pose and apply the shape model, resulting in 3D reconstructions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in achieving accurate vehicle pose estimations and 3D reconstructions.

The task of answering complex questions based on a knowledge graph involves not only selecting relevant facts, but also creating the correct logical framework to connect them. This process is known as inference, and it is crucial for accurately answering questions that involve relationships that are not explicitly stated. However, current methods for generating logical inference paths are limited, as they either focus on a single step at a time or rely on a fixed set of templates. This approach can be inefficient when dealing with complex questions that require multiple inference paths. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that involves breaking down the inference process into two stages: the first stage involves generating a query graph that captures the underlying relationships, and the second stage involves selecting the most likely answer based on that graph. This two-stage approach allows us to efficiently explore different inference paths and improve the accuracy of our results. Our experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper outlines a novel approach to algebraic systems, which integrates polynomial composites and monoid domains through a unified framework. We demonstrate that these structures share a common basis and provide a foundational understanding of their fundamental properties. Additionally, we explore practical applications derived from this unifying theory, which encompass various interrelated concepts, including the solution of systems of equations, monoid domains, free monoids, and polynomial composites.

Entity disambiguation is a critical task in understanding vast amounts of data, which often consist of linked entities. The conventional method involves creating a complete graph and then performing operations, but this approach has limitations when dealing with real-time data. To overcome this, we have developed a streaming entity disambiguation system that can handle evolving graphs over time. Our system utilizes a knowledge graph and entity ranking algorithms to identify entities, which we have tested using a variety of datasets. The results show that our system performs well on static datasets but faces challenges when dealing with dynamic and large-scale streaming data. To further improve the performance, we have also investigated the use of different knowledge graph embeddings and entity ranking algorithms, which we have found to be effective.

This research is focused on investigating the one-loop oblique corrections arising from scalar supersymmetric models, specifically the MSSM, in relation to electroweak symmetry breaking. The investigation encompasses the S, T, and U parameters, as well as the M_W, alpha, and gamma_Z observables. The one-loop effective action is derived for the MSSM scalars, and the corresponding Feynman rules are explicitly stated. The resulting expressions for the oblique corrections are subsequently simplified in the decoupling limit, and their contributions are presented in a form that is suitable for numerical evaluation.

We propose a novel framework for generating novel views of dynamic scenes from static, monocular video input. Our approach hinges on two key components: first, it creates a dynamic 3D model of the scene, and then it renders the scene from different angles and positions. Our solution to this problem is facilitated by a new loss function that enables the creation of detailed, accurate scene models, and a method for aligning predicted and ground truth pose estimates. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this method when applied to both simple and complex dynamic scenes.

We establish the existence of weak, time-invariant solutions to a specific category of stochastic partial differential equations. These equations incorporate a semi-linear term that features a quadratic growth pattern. The underlying process is defined by a time-changed Wiener process with a time-horizon governed by a non-uniformly elliptic, unbounded and unbounded-from Below diffusion coefficient.

A stochastic process called the random grain model is used to describe a random field that varies across space and time. It is used to model a specific type of noise that appears in Burgers' equation. It is used to study a specific type of differential equation that involves a random field. It is used to derive a specific type of solution for this equation. This solution is used to show that a specific type of nonlinear function of the random field converges to a function that depends only on the spatial variable. This result is used to show that a specific type of partial differential equation that involves a random field has a specific type of solution that depends only on the spatial variable.

Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are being considered as a key technology for the next generation of wireless networks. RISs have the potential to be integrated into various wireless communication systems, including 6G networks. This paper provides an overview of the main characteristics and benefits of RIS-based communication systems, as well as their potential applications. It also discusses the main challenges associated with the design of RIS-based communication systems, including passive RIS design, active RIS design, and signal detection algorithms. The paper also explores the potential applications of RIS in various fields, including wireless communication, sensing, and machine learning. Additionally, it discusses the potential to integrate RIS with other emerging technologies, including terahertz communication, artificial intelligence, and quantum communication.

Stochastic multi-agent systems often exhibit complex behavior characterized by multiple stable states, transient phases, and dynamic trajectories. Accurate modeling of such systems typically necessitates the use of high-dimensional continuous-time Markov chains, which can be computationally demanding. In this study, we introduce a new method to simplify the description of multi-agent systems featuring regions of stability and instability. By leveraging the existence of stable equilibrium points and using the properties of stable regions, we develop a method to approximate the system's behavior with a lower-dimensional continuous-time Markov chain. We demonstrate the applicability of this method to a specific model of bacterium Populations and validate its effectiveness through numerical simulations.

Deep neural networks are typically trained using high-precision floating-point numbers and then converted to lower-precision integers for deployment on devices. Current methods for training neural networks on low resource devices are limited to training with high precision and then optimizing to lower precision, known as one-pass training. However, this method is inefficient as it requires high precision during the training process. This research presents a new approach called Cyclic Training with Multiple Quantization Steps (CTMQ), enabling training and deployment on low precision devices in a single step. CTMQ trains the network with an initial high precision for a set number of iterations, then reduces precision to lower integer representations, and repeats this process alternating between the two precisions up to a set number of total iterations. This cycle allows the network to adapt to both precision types, resulting in improved performance. CTMQ is demonstrated to be effective on a range of mobile devices, including the Google Pixel 2 and the NVIDIA Jetson TX2, resulting in improved performance on tasks such as image classification and object detection.

The progenitor models of type Ia supernovae are still being extensively studied, with various theories suggesting that they originate from single stars or binary systems. A particular binary formation theory, known as the double-degenerate channel, proposes that type Ia supernovae arise from the explosion of a white dwarf-star binary system. This theory is supported by observations of supernovae 2011fe and 2014a, which exhibit distinct characteristics. A new study presents a new binary evolution channel for type Ia supernovae, which involves the coalescence of a white dwarf-star binary system with a massive main-sequence star. This process leads to the formation of a low-mass main-sequence star, which subsequently undergos a near-Chandrasekhar-mass type Ia supernova. This theory is supported by observations of SN 2017msl, which shares similar characteristics with other near-Chandrasekhar-mass type Ia supernovae. A particular binary evolution model, which involves the coalescence of a white dwarf-star binary system with a main-sequence companion, is found to be consistent with the observed properties of SN 2017msl. This model predicts that SN 2017msl would have a relatively low helium abundance and a high oxygen abundance, consistent with the observed data. This binary evolution channel provides an alternative explanation for the observed properties of SN 2017msl and may account for a significant fraction of type Ia

In a setting where data arrives incrementally, we investigate the potential for improved performance by incorporating unlabeled data into supervised models that are trained with labeled data. We explore how to leverage unlabeled data within existing models, specifically through the transfer of knowledge from a pre-existing model to a new, related one. We show that this approach can be used to enhance the performance of machine learning models, even when given only a small amount of unlabeled data, and demonstrate its potential for benefits in classification tasks, particularly in those with a large number of classes. Additionally, we introduce a new method for incorporating unlabeled data that is effective in a wide range of conditions and can be used to improve the performance of models across various types of classification problems.

The COVID-19 pandemic has presented a significant challenge for the world, with vaccination now emerging as a viable solution to combat the virus. Although the vaccination process itself is straightforward, the management of vaccination registration and tracking is a complex task that requires efficient and secure mechanisms. To address this issue, we propose a decentralized solution based on blockchain technology to streamline and accelerate the vaccination registration and monitoring process.

A significant issue in machine learning is determining whether class labels provide sufficient guidance for training neural networks, given that they are often imprecise, vague, and subject to variation. Our research involves analyzing the internal structure of class labels using a clustering approach to understand their underlying organization and relationships. Our findings reveal that even in large, complex datasets, classes can be grouped into distinct clusters, which in turn are influenced by the network's depth and the presence of noise in the data. These results have important implications for neural network training and the role of human oversight in mitigating the negative consequences of noisy labels.

We have developed a new method to describe the behavior of electrons in 2D materials through a mathematical framework based on broken symmetry and electron interactions. This approach, which is an expansion of a mathematical concept called loop expansion, allows us to accurately describe the behavior of electrons in these materials, even when they are subjected to certain interactions. By using this method, we are able to derive a set of equations that accurately capture the effects of electron interactions, which are not accounted for in other established theories. This allows us to make more accurate predictions about the behavior of electrons in these materials, which is not possible with other methods. We have applied this method to a specific type of material and found that it provides a more accurate description of electron interactions, which is consistent with previous research. This method has the potential to be applied to a broader range of materials and help to resolve some of the discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental results.

We have conducted a theoretical analysis of the spin-rotation collective excitation in strongly magnetized electron plasmas and found that its decay rate is influenced by the hyperfine interaction. The decay is caused by the transfer of magnetization through collisions between electrons and the crystal lattice. The resulting formula for the decay rate is similar to the one obtained for spin waves in ferromagnets, but it also takes into account the effects of strong magnetic fields on the plasma. The decay rate is also affected by the properties of the crystal lattice and the number of electrons in the plasma.

In a study of conformal Floquet dynamics, we investigate how continuous driving affects the behavior of conformal field theories (CFTs) when subjected to a periodic transformation. We analyze the impact of this process on the thermal properties of 2D CFTs and their correlation functions. We find that the thermal correlation functions of these CFTs can be precisely calculated using a method derived from the Jacobi theta function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the thermal entropy of a 2D CFT in a toroidal space follows a periodic evolution, with its maximum value determined by the thermal length of the system.

A novel sensor fusion approach is introduced, which unifies diverse sensor types, such as visual, inertial, and auditory, into a unified latent representation. This method enables a seamless integration of new sensor types, and is applied to a learning-based navigation system utilizing audio-visual inertial fusion. In contrast to conventional approaches, which typically focus on a single sensor type, our method combines multimodal sensory data to enhance robustness and accuracy. Through extensive testing on simulated and real-world audio-visual inertial datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of our method in terms of robustness against adverse conditions, and its ability to learn and adapt to new, unseen scenes.

The $\phi_s$'s decay width is influenced by the mass of the $b$ quark, and its magnitude is affected by the properties of the $B^0_s$ meson. The $\phi_s$'s decay width is also influenced by the decay of the $B^0_s$ meson into two jets, which is known as the hadronic decay. The $\Delta\Gamma_s$ represents the difference between the decay of the $B^0_s$ meson into two light quarks and its decay into two heavy quarks, which is a result of the interference of two key processes, $b\to c\bar c d - b\to c\bar c d\bar d$. The $\Delta\Gamma_s$ can be measured by analyzing the decay of the $B^0_s$ meson into two light quarks. The $\Delta\Gamma_s$ is a key observable in particle physics that can be used to test the standard model and the properties of the $B^0_s$ meson. This paper explores distributed optimal control of controlled graph systems with symmetric structures. We introduce a novel method for distributing an optimal control problem across interconnected agents, where each agent can only locally access the linear system and its neighbors. We transform the distributed problem into an equivalent centralized one, where the entire system is described using a single, combined matrix constructed using matrix filters and convolution. We then apply existing centralized solutions to the distributed problem, where each agent can calculate its local solution using its own filters and convolution. We demonstrate the accuracy of our method in a specific example involving an optimal linear quadratic regulator.

This study introduces a novel sensor management approach that jointly estimates the birth rates of new targets and labeled random sets, used for tracking multiple targets. A type of mixed integer linear programming called multi-sensor adaptive birth sampler is proposed, which optimizes the selection of sensors to use and the time to use each sensor, under a constraint on the expected number of measurements per time step. A type of optimization problem known as a mixed integer quadratic program, with a non-convex objective function, is used to find the optimal solution to the sampling problem. A type of optimization algorithm called branch and bound is used to find the optimal solution to the sampling problem. A simulation study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed sampling algorithm.

Linguists have been collecting language characteristics for a long time, but the process of gathering these traits for many languages is extremely time-consuming and labor-intensive. To address this, the 2020 SIGTYP shared task was organized around the idea of automating the collection of these traits using data-driven methods. The task focused on predicting various characteristics of over 200 languages, including morphological features such as polysynthesis, grammatical structure, and word order. The participants were given access to a dataset containing 223 languages and asked to develop systems for predicting these characteristics, with the top performers achieving an F1 score of 0.73.

A critical component in reinforcement learning is off-policy evaluation, which assesses the effectiveness of a given policy without compromising the stability of the underlying Markov decision process. This area has garnered significant attention in the field of reinforcement learning, with recent breakthroughs in deep learning and causal inference leading to numerous methods being developed for off-policy evaluation. This paper provides a thorough review of off-policy evaluation, categorizing relevant methods into four distinct groups and evaluating their advantages and limitations. Furthermore, we discuss the common challenges associated with off-policy evaluation and identify key areas for future research.

In biomanufacturing, a key challenge arises when producing a product through a series of connected tasks, with insufficient historical data to accurately determine the ideal time to harvest before quality degradation. This problem can be framed as an optimal stopping issue, necessitating a solution that balances minimal inventory costs with the need to avoid producing subpar products. However, existing optimal stopping algorithms are often based on the premise of abundant past data, a scenario rarely encountered in real-world scenarios. This paper addresses this limitation by developing a two-stage Bayesian approach that incorporates process variation, a crucial factor in determining product quality. The proposed method is then tested using a simulation, where it is compared to the optimal stopping theory benchmark, a heuristic approach found in industry, and a naive strategy of producing a fixed quantity of products at set points. The results demonstrate the superiority of the new method in terms of both profit maximization and product quality.

For a strongly coupled polarons, we establish tight, tightest-known upper bounds to the optimal polaron band structure. Our approach involves a direct minimization strategy to obtain these bounds, which corresponds to the minimization of the free energy of the system under given total energy constraints. This method is analogous to the variational method in condensed matter physics. Our findings show that these bounds are indeed optimal when the total energy is held constant, as demonstrated by their accuracy in limiting cases. Moreover, we observe that these bounds are asymptotically precise for both short and long wavelengths.

In the context of strongly-correlated systems, a plasma's long-wavelength behavior can be accurately described using holography. We examine the force-free solution of an electromagnetic plasma in a strongly-correlated state, focusing on its non-conducting state at zero temperature. We analyze the solution's stability and its behavior at large distances from the plasma, as well as its behavior near the plasma's surface. A key finding is that the solution's stability depends on a specific parameter, and that the solution can become unstable when this parameter falls below a certain threshold. Additionally, we find that the plasma's surface exhibits a specific property, and that the solution approaches a certain simplified form at large distances from the plasma.

We propose a new interpretation of the Schr\"odinger's cat thought experiment, which we call the "quantum complementarity paradigm." This interpretation posits that the classical state of the cat serves as a special kind of property that cannot be measured simultaneously with the wave state of the cat. This idea is rooted in the concept of "strong complementarity," which states that any property measured in one context cannot be measured in another context. This idea is not new and has been applied to various physical contexts, but it remains unexplored in the context of quantum biology. Through a series of logical steps, we demonstrate that the quantum complementarity paradigm is consistent with the principles of quantum mechanics and the laws of thermodynamics. This includes the possibility of the wave state of the cat influencing the wave state of its genetic material, which could lead to the birth of "quantum offspring." Furthermore, we suggest that the quantum complementarity paradigm could be experimentally tested using a modified version of the Schr\"odinger's cat thought experiment, which we call the "quantum complementarity experiment." This experiment would involve measuring the property of the cat's hunger while its wave state is entangled with a "quantum hunger particle." The results of this experiment would provide evidence for the quantum complementarity paradigm, which would have significant implications for our understanding of quantum biology.

This research introduces a novel geometric concept, the nonexpansive line, and establishes connections between periodic decomposition, nonexpansive lines, and other established notions like as (5; 10)-sets, Inradius, and Euler-Poincare characteristic. Nonexpansive lines are shown to be present in compact convex sets, with their maximum count tied to the Euler-Poincare characteristic and inradius, yielding optimal upper bounds. Furthermore, in simply connected convex bodies, nonexpansive lines are found to be limited in number and always occur in pairs, with their count related to the Euler-Poincare characteristic and inradius. Periodic decomposition is also explored in relation to convex polytopes, demonstrating that such polytopes can be decomposed into nonexpansive lines, with each decomposition resulting in a limited number of such lines.

This paper explores the connection between the Gromov-Hausdorff distance and Borsuk numbers. As a result, we can deduce that if the Borsuk problem has a negative solution for any metric space with a finite dimension $n$, it must also apply to Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.

In the context of homogenization, we've developed a more accurate approximation method for the resolvent of fourth-order operators under periodic conditions. This improvement is achieved by merging the resolvent with a pseudodifferential operator, and leveraging existing approximations for second-order operators as well as established Lp estimates. This approach yields an approximation of the resolvent with an error rate of O(ε^(-2)) in L2 norms in the homogenized direction, and can be adapted for use with other differential operators.

Recent advancements in multilingual task-oriented dialogue systems have been notable, yet the impact of language diversity on system performance remains under-explored. This study delves into the relationship between language proficiency and dialogue history, examining how different languages influence the accuracy of intent classification. Our analysis reveals that language-specific word embeddings outperform monolingual ones, and we propose a novel model, HistBERT, which leverages dialogue history to improve contextual understanding and enhance task-oriented dialogue systems. Experimental results demonstrate that HistBERT consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art models across various evaluation metrics in both English and non-English dialogue datasets.

Solving problems using SMT solving tools is a common practice in various fields, but the direct access to these tools often requires low-level API calls, which can hinder the integration of SMT solving into other applications. To address this issue, the Smt-Switch project was developed as a portable and versatile interface to different SMT solvers, allowing for a more streamlined interaction with these tools and making it easier to leverage their capabilities in a wide range of contexts.

This study presents a novel approach to quasi-exactly solvable systems, focusing on the application of moments theory to analyze the properties of these systems. The analysis is conducted on two specific models: the sextic anharmonic oscillator and the Bender-Dunne potential. The research demonstrates that the moments theory provides a valuable framework for examining the underlying characteristics of these systems, including the distribution of eigenvalues, the structure of the R-matrix, and the asymptotic behavior of the wave functions. The study also reveals that the moments theory offers a unified perspective on the sextic anharmonic oscillator and the Bender-Dunne potential, highlighting their shared features and underlying connections. Furthermore, the research shows that the moments theory enables the derivation of multiple QES bases for the sextic anharmonic oscillator and the Bender-Dunne potential, each corresponding to distinct symmetry groups. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of quasi-exactly solvable systems and their associated quasi-exactly solvable bases.

In computer vision, high-performance deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are typically large and computationally intensive, making them challenging to deploy on limited-capacity devices. To address this issue, researchers have been focusing on compact CNNs that achieve a balance between accuracy and resource constraints. However, these studies have often prioritized model size over image quality, leading to suboptimal outcomes. This paper proposes a novel approach that leverages high-resolution images to enhance CNN performance while maintaining a constant amount of model parameters or computational complexity. The experimental results demonstrate that this strategy yields a notable accuracy boost, with a notable 4.9% improvement in the ResNet-50 model on ImageNet when using 384x384 images instead of 224x224, despite a minimal increase in model parameters of 0.4%.

The DART mission's impact on asteroid Dimorphos is a unique opportunity to study the effects of external forces on binary asteroids. Specifically, the rotations of the components in a binary system create centrifugal forces that can cause motion on smaller objects, similar to the yoyo effect. This motion can be influenced by the shape and mass distribution of the components, as well as their orbital characteristics. Research suggests that the DART impact may create a crater on Dimorphos that is larger than expected, indicating that the secondary component bounces back to a point beyond the initial impact site. This bouncing effect is dependent on Dimorphos' moment of inertia, and simulations show that the yoyo effect is more likely to occur if this value is high.

This study explores the possibility of forming stable scalar clouds in the vicinity of a Reissner-Nordstrom black hole with a constant scalar field. We discovered that a black hole with a sufficiently large charge can support a stable cloud of particles with a scalar field that matches the field of the black hole. We also found that a four-dimensional complex scalar field can be regular and stationary at the black hole event horizon, which contradicts existing no-hair theorems for small and extremely large charges. However, our results align with these theorems for charges above a certain threshold.

The minimal extension of the Standard Model involving three heavy sterile neutrinos provides an explanation for the observed atmospheric and solar neutrino oscillations. The mixing between active and sterile neutrinos can be measured in experiments, and this mixing can be used to constrain the parameters of the model. The model's validity can be tested by testing its compliance with the observed neutrino oscillations, and this can be done by testing it against the observed neutrino oscillations at various energy scales. The model's parameters can be constrained by testing its compliance with the observed neutrino oscillations at different energy scales, and this can be done by testing it against the observed neutrino oscillations at different energy scales.
